title: Orgkey patterns & capacity demo - Heliotrope Retail
summary: Redwood AE+SE walked Heliotrope through org vs project key patterns, quota slicing, burst pools and console actions. Customer is evaluating for pilot in Q1 2028, main concerns: SSO/KMS, predictable latency for checkout flows, and cost controls across 20 teams.
next_steps: Redwood to share SOC2 + security pack and KMS integration notes
Maya to provision 2-week pilot keys and starter quota template
Customer to send sample traffic profile and success criteria by 2027-11-10
action_items: Maya Chen - Send SOC2 + security pack (due 2027-11-04)
Liam O'Connor - Create pilot org/project key config and example quota slices (due 2027-11-05)
Carlos Mendes - Export and share 2 weeks of token-level traffic profile (due 2027-11-10)
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-11-02
Time: 16:00 PST (46 mins)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendes (Heliotrope), Priya Rao (Heliotrope SRE), Evan Kline (Heliotrope CTO)

[00:00] Maya Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for carving out time. Quick agenda — we'll demo org- and project-key patterns in the Console, run through quota slices, show how burst pools and fairburst work, and then Liam will jump into a short Optimize recommendations walkthrough. Any additions?

[00:15] Carlos Mendes: Nope that sounds good. Main thing for us is predictable checkout latency for black friday kind of spikes and, um, making sure we don't blow the budget across business units.

[00:28] Liam O'Connor: Totally, that's the common tradeoff — latency versus unit cost. We'll show a couple of patterns that give you deterministic SLOs for critical routes while letting non-critical teams operate on cheaper models or lower priority lanes.

[00:40] Priya Rao: Quick question before we start — we run in GCP us-east and also have an on-prem reporting cluster. Do you support VPC/private deployment for any PII-handling models?

[00:48] Maya Chen: Yes. Redwood Private supports VPC and on-prem; you'll get a customer-managed control plane, KMS integrations for encryption, and audit logs. We'll attach the security pack after this call.

[00:58] Evan Kline: Do you have any gotchas around KMS — like bringing our own keys into the private control plane?

[01:05] Liam O'Connor: We support both BYOK and cloud KMS options. The console page we'll show has the KMS toggle in the security section — it's straightforward, but we'll include the exact steps in the security pack.

[01:20] Maya Chen: Alright, switching to the Console. (screen share) Here's an org we set up for this demo, name it heliotrope-demo. At the org level you can define default quotas and routing policy. Then you create projects — think of projects as teams or applications — each with its own project key.

[01:45] Maya Chen: Example pattern one: 'Org-managed quotas with project carve-outs.' You keep a global concurrency quota for the org that enforces total tokens/sec and concurrent requests; then carve out per-project slices for predictable minimum capacity. So e.g., checkout-service gets a reserved slice of 30% and marketing-experiments get 5%.

[02:05] Carlos Mendes: If marketing spikes, does that hurt checkout?

[02:08] Liam O'Connor: No — because the reserved slice ensures checkout gets the capacity it needs. Marketing can borrow from unused org capacity if available, but we enforce backpressure when org quotas are saturated. There's also a 'sticky routing' option so traffic from a project continues to route to the same model variant to keep cache locality.

[02:25] Priya Rao: You said backpressure — how is that surfaced to the client? HTTP 429?

[02:29] Liam O'Connor: Correct. We return standard 429 with headers that indicate quota bucket and retry-after. For streaming endpoints we gracefully finish the in-flight token stream then stop. We can also auto-fallback to a lower-cost variant instead of 429 — configurable per-route.

[02:50] Maya Chen: Pattern two is 'Project-first keys with centralized billing'. Teams get project keys; the org-level policy imposes quotas and rate limits. This gives teams autonomy for keys and RBAC while central finance can stitch billing reports by project or route.

[03:10] Evan Kline: How do you recommend we map microservices? We have ~20 teams and many ephemeral feature branches that also call the API.

[03:18] Liam O'Connor: For 20 teams, a two-tier approach usually works: org-level quotas + team project keys for day-to-day isolation. For ephemeral branches, use short-lived tokens or tag requests by branch metadata and apply a small shared dev quota so you don't need thousands of keys. We can show examples in the pilot config.

[03:40] Carlos Mendes: Cost controls — can we set token spend caps per project?

[03:44] Maya Chen: Yes. In the Console you can set monthly spend caps and hard stops. We also have soft alerts so the AE or billing owner gets pinged. Spend caps can be enforced at the project or org level.

[03:58] (screen change) Liam O'Connor: Now showing quota slice UI. You can create a slice, name it, set guarantees, maximums, and priority. Note the 'burst pool' toggle — this lets projects consume temporary burst capacity from a shared pool when their slice is exhausted, subject to fairness windows.

[04:20] Priya Rao: That burst pool — is it token-based or concurrency-based?

[04:23] Liam O'Connor: Both. You can carve pools in token units or request concurrency. For checkout we typically recommend guaranteeing concurrency for the lowest latencies, and enabling a token burst pool for occasional surges.

[04:38] Carlos Mendes: How do you prevent a noisy neighbor from draining the burst pool for weeks?

[04:42] Liam O'Connor: We enforce a sliding-window fairness algorithm — 'fairburst' — that decays burst credits over time. Also you can set per-project max-burst allocations and per-window throttles. If needed, you can also pin models to tiers and require approvals for large bursts.

[05:05] Maya Chen: Quick call-out: our analytics show that prefix/KV caching can reduce token spend by up to ~40% for conversational workloads. For checkout flows you might benefit less from prefix cache but the serving runtime supports compact KV caches for cart-state hot-paths.

[05:25] Evan Kline: You mentioned sticky routing earlier. If checkout traffic is sticky to a low-latency variant, what happens when that variant is full? Do you failover?

[05:33] Liam O'Connor: Failover policies are configurable. We can do immediate fallback to a warm compatible variant, or queue briefly, or route to a lower-cost variant depending on your SLO. For checkout we'd set aggressive fallback to preserve success but maybe slightly higher latency.

[05:50] (noise) Priya Rao: Sorry can you repeat the K-V thing? I heard K-V cash.

[05:54] Maya Chen: (laughs) K-V cache — key-value cache. We'll include examples of what to cache in the docs.

[06:05] Liam O'Connor: Moving to the API — here's an example request with an org key versus project key. Note the headers: x-org-id, x-project-id, and x-client-route. Those are used by our routing layer to reconcile quotas. If you send both org and project keys the project key overrides for per-route limits.

[06:30] Carlos Mendes: For SSO and RBAC, can we restrict which teams can create project keys?

[06:34] Maya Chen: Yes — RBAC controls are first-class. Admins can limit who can create keys, rotate them, and who can change quotas. We support SCIM provisioning and SAML SSO for user access.

[06:50] Liam O'Connor: Now jumping into Optimize suggestions — (share) the tool analyzes token distribution and suggests batching and quantization profiles per route. For example, non-interactive summarization routes get a recommendation to batch up to 8 requests with quantization Q4_8 to cut unit cost by ~30%.

[07:10] Priya Rao: Does that affect latency on checkout? No. Keep checkout on single-request low-latency path.

[07:14] Liam O'Connor: Exactly — you can pin certain routes to low-latency execution and exclude them from batching. Optimize will generate per-route config snippets you can import.

[07:30] Evan Kline: Any reporting on which project is causing tail-latency?

[07:34] Maya Chen: Redwood Console has per-key and per-route latency histograms. You can drill down to tokens, traces, and we provide traces that link back to sample payloads (PII redacted).

[07:50] (15 min mark – paraphrasing demo actions)

[08:05] Liam O'Connor: Quick tech deep-dive — runtime picks kernels based on model sequence length and HW; we do continuous batching in the runtime but honor concurrency guarantees by preemptive allocation. This reduces tail latency compared to naive batch queues.

[08:25] Carlos Mendes: For on-prem, is the same runtime used?

[08:28] Liam O'Connor: Yes, same runtime binary. The orchestration differs — you manage VPC networking and we provide a private control plane and optional support for HA with your infra team.

[08:40] Priya Rao: How do you handle audit logging and retention? We have 7-year requirements for some logs.

[08:46] Maya Chen: Audit logs are configurable; for Private deployments you can forward logs to your SIEM and set retention policies. We'll include recommended retention configurations in the security pack.

[09:00] (Customers ask for a concrete pilot plan)

[09:02] Maya Chen: Proposed pilot — 2-week sandbox org with 3 project keys: checkout, personalization, experiments. We'll pre-seed quota slices: checkout 40% reserved, personalization 20%, experiments 10%, org shared pool 30% with a token-based burst pool. We'll run a synthetic spike sim and a replay of your sample traffic.

[09:25] Carlos Mendes: That sounds reasonable. What do you need from us?

[09:28] Liam O'Connor: A traffic export — token/time series + per-route labels — and your success criteria: max p95 latency for checkout and acceptable fallbacks for degraded modes. Also the list of teams and who should get project keys.

[09:44] Evan Kline: Timeline — we want to evaluate in Q1 2028; pilot in December would be ideal to baseline before the new year.

[09:52] Maya Chen: We'll aim to get pilot keys out in one week.

[10:00] (wrap-up and confirmation of next steps)

[10:05] Maya Chen: Recap — we'll send SOC2/security pack, Liam will post the pilot quota template, and we'll provision demo keys. Action items are in the notes. Any other questions?

[10:18] Priya Rao: One last — is there a simple billing export to tie back to BigQuery?

[10:22] Maya Chen: Yes, billing exports to GCS/BigQuery are supported for Hosted and Dedicated. For Private, we emit usage files you can ingest.

[10:30] Carlos Mendes: Great — thanks everyone.

[10:34] Maya Chen: Thanks, we'll follow up with the docs and next steps. Bye.

(End of transcript)
